title: A Carol Video a Day
footer: One Christmas carol a day, December 1 to 24, ending with Silent Night on Christmas Eve. Every link goes to the performer's or label's own YouTube channel, and all music and videos belong to their owners.

entries.title: Once in Royal David's City
entries.blurb: Traditionally the first carol of the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols at King's College, with the opening verse sung by a single treble.

entries.title: O Come, O Come, Emmanuel
entries.blurb: An Advent hymn of longing, based on the medieval 'O Antiphons'.

entries.title: Deck the Halls
entries.blurb: Fa-la-la-la-la. The melody comes from an old Welsh New Year's tune, 'Nos Galan'.

entries.title: Carol of the Bells
entries.blurb: Built on 'Shchedryk', a Ukrainian folk chant arranged by Mykola Leontovych. This version is played on violin.

entries.title: Good King Wenceslas
entries.blurb: Saint Wenceslaus, Duke of Bohemia, braves the snow on St Stephen's Day to help a poor man. The words are by John Mason Neale.

entries.title: The First Noel
entries.blurb: A traditional English carol about the shepherds and the star, sung a cappella.

entries.title: God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen
entries.blurb: One of the oldest carols still widely sung. Dickens quotes it in A Christmas Carol.

entries.title: O Tannenbaum
entries.blurb: The German 'O Christmas Tree' as jazz piano, from the 1965 soundtrack of A Charlie Brown Christmas.

entries.title: Angels We Have Heard on High
entries.blurb: A French carol, 'Les Anges dans nos campagnes', famous for its long 'Gloria in excelsis Deo' refrain.

entries.title: Away in a Manger
entries.blurb: A lullaby carol first published in America in the late 1800s.

entries.title: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear
entries.blurb: Written by Edmund Sears in Massachusetts in 1849.

entries.title: Ding Dong Merrily on High
entries.blurb: Words by George Ratcliffe Woodward, set to a lively 16th-century French dance tune.

entries.title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
entries.blurb: An African-American spiritual, collected and published by John Wesley Work Jr.

entries.title: We Wish You a Merry Christmas
entries.blurb: A traditional English carol from the West Country. Bring on the figgy pudding.

entries.title: In the Bleak Midwinter
entries.blurb: A poem by Christina Rossetti, set to music by Gustav Holst.

entries.title: The Little Drummer Boy
entries.blurb: Written in 1941 by Katherine Kennicott Davis, originally as 'Carol of the Drum'. Pa-rum-pum-pum-pum.

entries.title: Joy to the World
entries.blurb: Words by Isaac Watts (1719). Whitney's gospel version is from The Preacher's Wife.

entries.title: What Child Is This?
entries.blurb: William Chatterton Dix's 1865 words set to 'Greensleeves'. Recorded live at the Kodak Theatre in 2009.

entries.title: O Little Town of Bethlehem
entries.blurb: Written by Phillips Brooks, inspired by his visit to Bethlehem in 1865.

entries.title: Adeste Fideles
entries.blurb: The Latin original of 'O Come, All Ye Faithful', usually credited to John Francis Wade in the 1700s.

entries.title: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
entries.blurb: Charles Wesley's words, a tune adapted from Mendelssohn, and David Willcocks's soaring descant.

entries.title: Coventry Carol
entries.blurb: A haunting 16th-century English carol from the Coventry mystery plays, sung by the Irish choir Anúna.

entries.title: O Holy Night
entries.blurb: 'Minuit, chrétiens' by Adolphe Adam, 1847. Fall on your knees.

entries.title: Silent Night
entries.blurb: First sung on Christmas Eve 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria. Words by Joseph Mohr, music by Franz Gruber.
